title: AFCA flags authorisation breaches, poor licensee oversight
full_text:
The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) has identified several systemic issues in the investment and advice sector in the ninth edition of its systemic issues report.
Drawing on AFCA’s data and information provided by financial firms during investigations, the latest Systemic Issues Insights Report by the complaints authority noted concerns about investment activity extending beyond the authority provided by clients.
AFCA said it is concerned about what happens after advice is given, and whether advisers implement the agreed strategy and stay fully within the client’s authority.
For instance, an advice file can look compliant on paper, but the client’s investments can subsequently be traded or managed in a way they never authorised.
Examples include options trading without authority, transactions outside a client’s mandate and failure to properly implement advice to reduce or exit higher-risk investments.
This raises underlying issues of conflicts of interest, as well as the misrepresentation of investment risk and performance.
“Client authority should therefore be considered as an ongoing control rather than a one-off administrative step at the beginning of the advice relationship,” the report said.
A solution, as suggested by AFCA, would be for the adviser to give clear evidence of client authority before transactions are implemented.
Meanwhile, the report also identified issues with weak supervision of advisers and authorised representatives (ARs) by licensees.
The main point is that licensees may have monitoring systems that are not strong enough to detect inappropriate or misleading advice, unauthorised activity, complex/high-risk strategies, as well as advice that doesn’t match a client’s circumstances.
AFCA argued that supervision needs to be risk-based, with greater scrutiny of complex strategies, concentrated or illiquid investments, SMSFs, unusual transactions and advisers with significant discretion.
“Effective supervision… involves understanding whether the advice and resulting consumer outcomes remain consistent with the client’s circumstances, objectives and agreed strategy,” the report said.
When a concern does emerge, it said firms should look for similar conduct across other clients and assess whether it points to a broader issue.
Earlier this year, AFCA had seen a rise in complaints related to managed accounts. Senior ombudsman Nick Batard said managed accounts-related complaints were up 25 per cent, and while the actual number was arguably low (10), it highlighted growing concern in how some advisers are using them.
Meanwhile, the Financial Services Council (FSC) made a series of recommendations it believes would improve the current financial advice licensing system. One of them was to combine AFCA complaint trends with other data, such as adviser movements, insurance claims and regulatory reports, to identify potential risks early and trigger further investigation or closer supervision.
